bibl.title: Functional organization of mouse auditory cortex in response to stimulus complexity and brain state

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Three new regions responsive to high-frequency tones and four new gradients responsive to frequency modulations (FMs) were identified.

span.label: tonotopic and FM-sweep-rate maps in mouse auditory cortex
span.quote: The present study aimed to assess the mouse auditory cortex (AC) responses under varying conditions of stimulus complexity and brain state.

span.label: wide-field-calcium-imaging
span.quote: In this study, we used wide-field Ca2+ imaging through a large cranial window in a transgenic mouse that expresses the genetically encoded calcium indicator GCaMP6 (Nakai et al., 2001; Iadecola, 2004; Tian et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2013; Cramer et al., 2019).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Isoflurane reduces cochlear blood flow, blocks acetylcholine receptors and enhances GABA-gated currents, which raises medial olivocochlear efferent inhibition and so depresses auditory sensitivity in the anesthetized state
span.quote: The possible mechanisms underlying these impacts are changes in cochlear blood flow (CBF) (Nakashima et al., 2003; Xiao et al., 2014), the blockage of acetylcholine (ACh) receptors (Dilger et al., 1992), and enhanced gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-gated channel currents (Ming et al., 2001), which lead to increased inhibition mediated by medial olivocochlear (MOC) efferents (Sheppard et al., 2018).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Behaviourally relevant high frequencies are over-represented in the mouse auditory cortex because the mouse hearing range extends much further upward, which is why the newly found regions are all high-frequency ones
span.quote: This finding suggests that the AC tonotopic maps are oriented more toward high frequencies than low frequencies, which is consistent with the wider spectrum of high frequencies in the mouse hearing range (Heffner, 1980).

span.label: Imaging was confined to the right auditory cortex, so lateralization of vocal processing could not be assessed.
span.note: what this limits: any lateralisation claim: A CRANIOTOMY WAS MADE ONLY OVER THE RIGHT AC
span.quote: In this study, a craniotomy was made only over the right AC.

span.label: Isoflurane was used as a model of the sleeping brain, and whether the state effects are anaesthetic or sleep-related is unresolved.
span.note: what this limits: the sleep interpretation of the state effects: REPLICATION OF OUR FINDINGS DURING NATURAL SLEEP WILL CLARIFY WHETHER CHANGES IN HEARING SENSITIVITY RESULT FROM USING ISOFLURANE OR ARE ASSOCIATED WITH SLEEP PROCESSES
span.quote: Replication of our findings during natural sleep will clarify whether changes in hearing sensitivity result from using isoflurane or are associated with sleep processes.

span.label: The comparison of natural sleep against awake and anaesthetized states is left to future work.
span.note: what this limits: the same scope as item 1: THE IMPACT OF SLEEP COMPARED TO ANESTHETIZED AND AWAKE STATES SHOULD BE STUDIED IN THE FUTURE
span.quote: The impact of sleep compared to anesthetized and awake states should be studied in the future.

span.label: The map of this cortex has been revised repeatedly, and the paper attributes the revisions to advances in technique rather than to new anatomy.
span.note: what this limits: any area label in the mouse auditory cortex literature: the paper states the tonotopic organisation of the belt area has been significantly updated as neuroimaging and recording advanced
span.quote: However, during the past decades, technological advancements in neuroimaging and recording have led to significant updates in the tonotopic organization of the belt area.

span.label: An area in the classical map is reported as dissolvable into parts of two others, on the evidence of one technique.
span.note: what this limits: the UF area as a unit in the mouse auditory map: electrophysiological measurements are reported as suggesting it should be considered subparts of AAF and AI
span.quote: For instance, electrophysiological measurements suggest the “UF” area should be considered as subparts of the AAF and AI

span.label: The tonotopic map rests on a per-frequency threshold identified by the experimenters.
span.note: what this limits: the tonotopic maps in this paper: for each frequency a threshold level was identified and used to determine the map
span.quote: For each frequency, the threshold level was identified (red squares) and used to determine the tonotopic map.

span.label: The paper's own account of why the map keeps changing is an account of instruments, not of findings - decades of technological advancement producing significant updates to the organisation. On that account the current map is the current technique's map, and the paper is adding a fourth.
span.quote: However, during the past decades, technological advancements in neuroimaging and recording have led to significant updates in the tonotopic organization of the belt area

span.label: tonotopic organization
span.quote: However, during the past decades, technological advancements in neuroimaging and recording have led to significant updates in the tonotopic organization of the belt area.

span.label: UF
span.quote: For instance, electrophysiological measurements suggest the “UF” area should be considered as subparts of the AAF and AI

span.label: AI
span.quote: Using multiscale optical Ca2+ imaging, it was shown that the AI area includes two rostral regions that process highfrequency tones

span.label: auditory cortex
span.quote: For each frequency, the threshold level was identified (red squares) and used to determine the tonotopic map

span.label: AI (primary auditory cortex) - AS ONE AREA in the classical map, versus as an area containing TWO high-frequency regions, which is what optical calcium imaging reported
span.quote: Using multiscale optical Ca2+ imaging, it was shown that the AI area includes two rostral regions that process highfrequency tones

span.label: AI (primary auditory cortex) - AND AS SPLIT DIFFERENTLY AGAIN by a third technique: flavoprotein autofluorescence with anatomy makes the dorsal high-frequency part a discrete region
span.quote: A recent publication on AC tonotopy, using a combination of flavoprotein autofluorescence imaging and anatomical techniques, demonstrated that AI includes two areas that respond to high-frequency tones and that the dorsal part of the AI high-frequency area is a discrete region from the rest of the AI

span.label: AI (primary auditory cortex) - AND AS PART OF A WHOLLY NEW LAYOUT: widefield calcium imaging in awake mice is reported as introducing a new layout for auditory cortex
span.quote: Using widefield calcium imaging in awake mice, Romero et al. (Romero et al., 2020) also introduced a new layout for AC

span.label: revision of the map - attributed by the paper to TECHNIQUE rather than to anatomy: 'technological advancements in neuroimaging and recording have led to significant updates in the tonotopic organization of the belt area'
span.quote: However, during the past decades, technological advancements in neuroimaging and recording have led to significant updates in the tonotopic organization of the belt area

span.label: contradicts → Issa et al. (2017), which reported no difference between upward and downward FM sweep maps
span.quote: Despite the report of no difference between upward and downward FM sweep maps in a previous study (Issa et al., 2017), we found that the center of the slow sweep rate responsive area in AI shifts 350 µm rostrally between upward and downward FM sweep maps.

span.label: extends → Issa et al. (2017), whose imaging window was too small to resolve map borders
span.quote: Among a few studies of mouse AC organization in encoding FM sweep rates, the Issa et al. (Issa et al., 2017) study suffers from a small imaging window, which makes it difficult to delineate the structure of the resulting maps near the imaging borders.

span.label: extends → Romero et al. (2020), whose VPAF is placed differently
span.quote: The VPAF region identified by Romero et al. (Romero et al., 2020) is in a different location and is primarily responsive to low frequencies.

span.label: builds-on → Issa et al. (2014) landmark-registration procedure
span.quote: The registration deformation field was constructed using landmarks from each experimental session and target landmarks as previously described in Issa et al. (Issa et al., 2014).

span.label: UF —part-of→ AI
span.note: differs in: WHICH TECHNIQUE IS ASKED. 'ELECTROPHYSIOLOGICAL MEASUREMENTS suggest the UF area should be considered as SUBPARTS of the AAF and AI' - so on that instrument UF is not an area at all but pieces of two others. The record already carries THREE readings of AI as senses, one per technique: optical calcium imaging splits it into two high-frequency regions, flavoprotein autofluorescence makes the dorsal part discrete, widefield imaging introduces a new layout entirely · strength of the relation: 0.7 — AN AREA THAT DISSOLVES INTO PARTS OF TWO OTHERS DEPENDING ON THE METHOD. The boundary is not a fact the techniques disagree about - each technique constitutes a different partition, and all of them are current.
span.quote: For instance, electrophysiological measurements suggest the “UF” area should be considered as subparts of the AAF and AI

span.label: tonotopic organization —operationalised-as→ auditory cortex
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — THE MAP RESTS ON A PER-FREQUENCY THRESHOLD THE EXPERIMENTERS IDENTIFY: 'For each frequency, THE THRESHOLD LEVEL WAS IDENTIFIED (red squares) and USED TO DETERMINE the tonotopic map.' The partition of the cortex is downstream of a decision made per frequency, which is worth having beside the three-way disagreement above.
span.quote: For each frequency, the threshold level was identified (red squares) and used to determine the tonotopic map

span.label: Kruskal-Wallis test
span.quote: A Kruskal-Wallis test at each pixel was applied to statistically compare the two tonotopic maps in their best frequency.

span.label: chi-squared goodness-of-fit test
span.quote: The Chi-square goodness-of-fit test was applied to assess if values of an array come from the same distribution.

span.label: bootstrap
span.quote: The bootstrap method was also used to generate a distribution of topographic maps for each animal and session of recording.

span.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
span.quote: To test whether the explained variance value for stimuli is greater than that of the behavioral measures and video, a one-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test was performed.

span.label: p-value
span.quote: Statistical significance was determined at a p-value < 0.05 for all statistical analyses.

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: The shaded error bars used in any figure represent the standard error of the mean (SEM).

span.label: regression
span.quote: To calculate the contribution of sound stimuli and other behavioral measures in the construction of the cortical signals, linear ridge regression was performed on each session of recording.

span.label: coefficient of determination
span.quote: For the linear model fitting of frequency or FM rate as a function of distance in a topographic gradient, the ‘fitlm’ function from MATLAB was applied and its adjusted R2 was reported.

span.label: explained variance
span.quote: To calculate the contribution of a set of predictors in the construction of wide-field cortical activity the explained variance (R2) map was determined in the following way.

span.label: singular value decomposition
span.quote: These PCs were the outputs of applying singular value decomposition (SVD) on the vectorized video frames.

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: The threshold was defined as 95 percentiles of the motion signal (equivalent to mean + 2×standard deviation but it is not sensitive to large value outliers).

span.label: Three previously uncharacterised tonotopic regions of mouse auditory cortex - the dorsal anterior field, the posterior auditory field and the ventral posterior auditory field - were identified, all preferentially responsive to high frequencies and lying dorsal and caudal to the known areas.
span.quote: The newly identified regions were generally responsive to higher frequencies and were in dorsal and caudal AC regions.

span.label: Tonotopic maps were stable within a single 25-minute session, across three consecutive weeks in the same mouse, and across the twelve animals.
span.quote: Except for a few sparse pixels, the tonotopic maps were quite similar over time and between animals.

span.label: High-frequency responses in AI-H and UF were larger in awake than in isoflurane-anesthetized mice, implying reduced high-frequency hearing sensitivity under anesthesia.
span.quote: In this study, the response amplitude at high frequencies (the H region of AI and UF) was greater in the tonotopic maps from awake compared to anesthetized mice.

span.label: Under anesthesia the cortical area encoding slow FM sweep rates expanded and the area encoding fast sweep rates shrank across AAF, DA and UF.
span.quote: The second difference was shown in the AAF-DA-UF regions, in which the response to slower sweep rates was expanded and the response to faster sweep rates was reduced in maps from the anesthetized compared to the awake state.

span.label: Contrary to an earlier report of no difference, upward and downward FM sweep maps do differ: the slow-rate centre in AI sits about 350 micrometres more rostral for downward sweeps.
span.quote: Despite the report of no difference between upward and downward FM sweep maps in a previous study (Issa et al., 2017), we found that the center of the slow sweep rate responsive area in AI shifts 350 µm rostrally between upward and downward FM sweep maps.

span.label: Ultrasonic vocalizations drove stronger responses than pure tones specifically in the regions tuned to fast FM sweep rates (AII, DP, PAF, VPAF and a zone between UF and AAF), and not in the high-frequency tonotopic regions.
span.quote: In our study, vocal stimuli elicited a stronger response than tonal stimuli in both anesthetized and awake states, and a higher V/T ratio was obtained in the regions (AII, DP, PAF, VPAF, and a region between UF and AAF) linked to the processing of faster FM sweep rates compared to regions that respond to high frequencies.

span.label: Best frequency changes with distance along a tonotopic gradient as a sigmoid: middle frequencies change steeply over a short stretch of cortex while low and high frequencies occupy longer stretches.
span.quote: This sigmoid function reflects steeper frequency changes in a shorter distance for middle frequencies versus lower and higher frequencies.

span.label: Tone-evoked cortical activity stays near its source, so tonotopic maps computed from any averaging window between 100 ms and 1000 ms after onset come out identical.
span.quote: This similarity demonstrates that in the AC regions tonal stimuli evoke spatiotemporal responses that do not travel far from their initial source locations.

span.label: The tonotopic map spans 2 mm rostro-caudally and 1.9 mm dorso-ventrally, so the conventional 2x2 mm imaging window used in earlier work is too small to capture all of it.
span.quote: The distance between the farthest landmarks in the tonotopic map supports the idea that a window larger than 2 mm in each axis is necessary to include all cortical regions involved in the AC tonotopic organization.

span.label: core auditory area
span.quote: The “core auditory area”, located at the center of the AC, consists of the primary auditory cortex (AI) and the anterior auditory field (AAF), with best frequency spatial gradients (tonotopic axes) that mirror each other

span.label: belt auditory region
span.quote: belt auditory region”, which is also known as the higher-order auditory area or secondary AC, is less-characterized in the literature and includes the secondary auditory field (AII), the ultrasonic field (UF), and the dorsoposterior field (DP).

span.label: tonotopic organization
span.quote: This tonotopic organization is characterized by a spectrum of gradients extended from neurons that preferentially respond to certain frequencies, ranging from high to low (Humphries et al., 2010).

span.label: frequency sweep rate
span.quote: The frequency sweep rate was calculated through the division of frequency coverage (5oct) by sweep duration.

span.label: V/T ratio (cortical response ratio of vocalizations to tones)
span.term: V/T ratio (cortical response ratio of vocalizations to tones)
span.quote: After excluding unresponsive pixels, the average response to USVs was divided by the average response to pure tones (V/T) for each animal.

span.label: responsive pixel
span.quote: A pixel was identified as responsive if its signal within a 1 s time window after stimulus onset was greater than the mean + 3×standard deviation of the baseline.

span.label: brain state (awake vs. isoflurane-anesthetized)
span.quote: Awake and isoflurane-anesthetized recordings were performed for 12 and 6 mice, respectively. Anesthetized recordings were performed with 1.0% isoflurane.

span.label: tone frequency and sound pressure level
span.term: tone frequency and sound pressure level
span.quote: Pure tones were generated at low (4 kHz), medium (11.3 kHz), and high (32 kHz) frequencies; and at low (40 dB), medium (60 dB), and high (80 dB) sound pressure levels (SPL).

span.label: FM sweep direction and sweep duration (rate)
span.term: FM sweep direction and sweep duration (rate)
span.quote: Both upward and downward frequency directions and 5 sweep durations with logarithmic increments between 10-500ms (i.e., 10, 27, 71, 188, and 500 ms) were applied.

span.label: best frequency per pixel
span.quote: A response weighted sum of these two frequencies was determined as the best frequency at any given pixel.

span.label: pixel responsiveness to sound
span.quote: Pixel responsiveness also was determined proportionally to the average response amplitudes at all threshold levels.

span.label: body temperature
span.quote: A heating pad was used throughout the recordings to maintain the mice's body temperature at 37°C.

span.label: sound pressure level of the FM stimuli
span.term: sound pressure level of the FM stimuli
span.quote: The FM stimuli were played only at 60 dB SPL, which was used as the sound pressure level for all sweep rates.

span.label: frequency coverage of the FM sweeps
span.term: frequency coverage of the FM sweeps
span.quote: For all FM stimuli, frequency coverage was constant in the 2-64 kHz (5oct) range and the SPL was set at 60dB.

span.label: spontaneous behaviour (nose, whisker-pad, mouth, body and forepaw motion plus behavioural-video components)
span.term: spontaneous behaviour (nose, whisker-pad, mouth, body and forepaw motion plus behavioural-video components)
span.quote: The predictors include stimuli features, behavioral events, and changes in the behavioral video.

span.label: 12 and 6 — Number of mice recorded awake and anesthetized respectively
span.quote: Awake and isoflurane-anesthetized recordings were performed for 12 and 6 mice, respectively.

span.label: R2 > 0.93 and 0.90 — Adjusted R-squared of the linear fit to the inverse-sigmoid frequency-distance relation, awake and anesthetized
span.quote: The associations were highly linear (R2 > 0.93 and 0.90 for awake and anesthetized states, respectively) and confirmed the sigmoid relationship between the best frequency and distance from the low-frequency landmark in a tonotopic gradient.

span.label: R2 > 0.95 and 0.87 — Fit quality of the inverse-sigmoid function for the FM sweep-rate/distance relation, awake and anesthetized
span.quote: A sigmoid function was obtained in the plots (Figures 6I and 6J for awake and anesthetized, respectively) after fitting an inverse-sigmoid function to each graph (R2 > 0.95 and 0.87 for awake and anesthetized states, respectively).

span.label: 1.36 and 1.51 — Median vocalization-to-tone response ratio in the USV-favouring pixels, awake and anesthetized
span.quote: The median values of the V/T ratio for the regions favoring USVs (i.e., pixels with V/T > 1) were 1.36 and 1.51 for awake and anesthetized states, respectively.

span.label: 2 mm and 1.9 mm — Extent of the auditory cortex tonotopic map along the rostral-caudal and dorsal-ventral axes
span.quote: The distance between the centers of the two farthest regions was 2 mm on the rostral-caudal axis and 1.9 mm on the dorsal-ventral axis.

span.label: AI-L p = 0.0054, AI-H p = 0.0171, AAF-L p = 0.0181, UF p = 0.0216, DP p = 0.0165 — Median p-values for the five regions whose best frequency differed between awake and anesthetized maps
span.quote: and DP (median p-values shown in S1C table: AI-L p = 0.0054, AI-H p = 0.0171, AAF-L p = 0.0181, UF p = 0.0216, DP p = 0.0165).

span.label: 350 µm — Rostral shift of the AI slow-sweep-rate landmark in the downward compared with the upward FM map
span.quote: In downward compared to upward sweep rate maps, the center of the slow sweep rate region in AI is shifted 350 µm rostrally.

span.label: 25 times — Repetitions of each frequency-SPL pair per imaging session
span.quote: Each frequency-SPL pair was played 25 times per imaging session.

span.label: 33.3ms (30 Hz) — Temporal resolution / frame rate of the wide-field calcium imaging
span.quote: For the mesoscale calcium imaging data collection, 12-bit images were captured with 33.3ms temporal resolution (30 Hz frame rate) with a charge-coupled device (CCD) camera

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.08.11.503675.
